newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Wringing gains from range-bound U.S..
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Wringing gains from range-bound U.S..

text.p: U.S. Treasury yields have been locked in a range since April and there is little prospect of a major breakout in the weeks ahead, despite renewed jitters over interest rates, analysts said on Monday.
Nevertheless, investors can still eke out gains from the U.S. market, analysts said.

"If you've got low and stable inflation rates that's what you're going to have to expect -- cycles with low amplitude where you have to trade tighter ranges to make money," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London.

"A lot of people have been waiting for 7.25 percent and 7.50 percent and have never seen it. There is the danger especially for the fund management community that if they wait too long they'll miss the slow down in the economy," he said.

The yield on 30-year Treasury bond nudged up to 7.0 percent in the U.S. on Monday after minutes from the Federal Reserve's July policy meeting revealed officials had shifted to tightening bias on interest rates.
Stonger-than-expected July durable goods orders did not help and the market was likely to remain addled ahead of purchasing manager and payroll data next week, analysts said.
But Monday's move on the long bond only put the yield back firmly in the middle of the 6.64 percent to 7.18 percent range it has been trading in since April.

While strong payroll data would increase the chances of a rate rise before the presidential elections in November, many analysts do not see one until the end of the year -- and they see tight ranges continuing.
Chase's Marshall said in a low inflation environment dramatic fluctuations in interest rates and bond yields may be a way of the past.

"The key thing to bear in mind is that it's wrong to expect a cycle where yields skyrocket to eight percent or they collapse to six percent," he said. "This tightening cycle may only be one or two moves."
Steve Major, Paris-based head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais, expects the Federal Reserve to remain on hold for the next three to four months. He would favour four-and-five year paper.
"I would be inclined to buy the middle of the curve, sell 18-month to two-year paper and sell the longer end," he said.
Selling the short-end would give yield pick-up while selling the long would reduce risk, he added.
Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London, is more negative on Treasuries, seeing strong August data, and a rate rise in September.
In such an environment, curve flattening trades and an outright move into cash would be judicious, he said. With the dollar expected to gain from a rate rise, an unhedged position would be best.
"The short-end is the worst place to be in terms of yield," he said. "Sub-six percent in terms of two-year is very, very expensive. The market is not braced for any tightening moves at all."
But while Chester said strong data next week might push the long bond yield back up to 7.25 percent, it would need a Fed tightening to crack that level and send the yield toward 7.5 percent.
